title: What are JPA entity lifecycle callbacks and when does each one fire?

s1_definition.profdef: JPA lifecycle callbacks are methods annotated to run automatically at specific points in an entity's persistence lifecycle: `@PrePersist`/`@PostPersist` around INSERT, `@PreUpdate`/`@PostUpdate` around UPDATE, `@PreRemove`/`@PostRemove` around DELETE, and `@PostLoad` after an entity is loaded from the database. They can live on the entity itself or in a separate listener class via `@EntityListeners`.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of these as automatic stamps National Bank of India puts on a form at each stage. `@PrePersist` is the stamp right before a brand new account form is filed ("set open date, generate reference"). `@PostPersist` is the confirmation stamp after filing. `@PreUpdate` stamps just before edits are saved ("set last-modified"). `@PreRemove` stamps before shredding ("mark closed, notify"). `@PostLoad` is what happens the moment a clerk pulls a file out of the cabinet to read it ("compute display fields"). Nobody tells the clerk each time — these happen automatically.
s1_definition.oneliner: Callbacks are automatic hooks that fire around insert, update, delete, and load — no manual calls needed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** JPA lifecycle callbacks are methods annotated to run automatically at specific points in an entity's persistence lifecycle: `@PrePersist`/`@PostPersist` around INSERT, `@PreUpdate`/`@PostUpdate` around UPDATE, `@PreRemove`/`@PostRemove` around DELETE, and `@PostLoad` after an entity is loaded from the database. They can live on the entity itself or in a separate listener class via `@EntityListeners`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of these as automatic stamps National Bank of India puts on a form at each stage. `@PrePersist` is the stamp right before a brand new account form is filed ("set open date, generate reference"). `@PostPersist` is the confirmation stamp after filing. `@PreUpdate` stamps just before edits are saved ("set last-modified"). `@PreRemove` stamps before shredding ("mark closed, notify"). `@PostLoad` is what happens the moment a clerk pulls a file out of the cabinet to read it ("compute display fields"). Nobody tells the clerk each time — these happen automatically.

**One line to remember:** Callbacks are automatic hooks that fire around insert, update, delete, and load — no manual calls needed.

sections.s2_technical:
`@PrePersist` runs before the INSERT is issued (actually before flush schedules it). For example, on a Transaction entity you can set the creation timestamp and generate a reference number here: `this.createdAt = Instant.now(); this.reference = "TXN-" + UUID...`. `@PostPersist` runs after the INSERT, when the generated id is available — good for firing an event or logging.

`@PreUpdate` runs before an UPDATE is flushed; typically you set `updatedAt`. Important nuance: it only fires if Hibernate's dirty checking actually detects a change — if nothing changed, no UPDATE and no PreUpdate. `@PostUpdate` runs after the UPDATE.

`@PreRemove` runs before the DELETE; use it to cascade soft-cleanup or raise a "record about to be deleted" event. `@PostRemove` runs after.

`@PostLoad` runs after the entity is populated from a query or find. This is the right place to compute transient/derived fields. For example, on an Account with transient `availableBalance = balance - holdAmount`, compute it in @PostLoad.

Senior nuances: callbacks must not call the EntityManager to perform new persistence operations (no new queries, no flush) — that is unsupported and risks recursion. Keep them side-effect-light. For cross-cutting logic across many entities, put callbacks in a shared listener class registered with `@EntityListeners(AuditListener.class)`; the listener methods take the entity as a parameter. The order is: for a new entity, PrePersist then (flush) then PostPersist; for load, PostLoad; for update, PreUpdate then PostUpdate.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Every new transaction at National Bank of India needs a creation timestamp and a unique reference like TXN-xxxx, and we keep forgetting to set them in the service code. This is exactly @PrePersist — it runs automatically right before the insert, guaranteeing the fields are always set.

Problem 2 — Whenever a transaction's status changes we must record when it was last modified. This is exactly @PreUpdate, which fires automatically before the update, but only when something actually changed.

Problem 3 — When we load an account we want to show the customer their available balance, which is current balance minus any held amount, but we do not store it. This is exactly @PostLoad — it computes derived fields the moment the entity is loaded.

Problem 4 — Before any account is deleted we must log it for audit. This is @PreRemove.

We will build a Transaction and an Account entity with these callbacks and demonstrate each firing.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -jar target/txn-lifecycle-service-1.0.0.jar

# Create a transaction (PrePersist/PostPersist fire)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/txns \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"id":"T1","amount":50000}'

# Settle it (PreUpdate fires)
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/api/v1/txns/T1/settle
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: create transaction T1 for 50,000, then settle it; separately load account SAV2001.

Step 1 — `new Transaction("T1", 50000)` creates a transient object with status PENDING but reference and createdAt still null.

Step 2 — `repo.save(t)` schedules an INSERT. Just before the insert, `@PrePersist onCreate()` fires, setting createdAt=now and reference=TXN-xxxx. The INSERT then carries those values.

Step 3 — After the INSERT, `@PostPersist afterCreate()` fires and logs the reference.

Step 4 — `settle("T1")` loads T1 and calls setStatus("SETTLED"). The status changed, so dirty checking marks it dirty. On flush, `@PreUpdate onUpdate()` fires setting updatedAt, then the UPDATE runs.

Step 5 — When account SAV2001 is loaded, `@PostLoad computeDerived()` fires and sets availableBalance = 1,000,000 - 50,000 = 950,000 (not stored, computed every load).

```
INFO  Transaction persisted: TXN-a1b2c3d4
INFO  Created T1 with ref TXN-a1b2c3d4
Hibernate: insert into transactions ...
Hibernate: update transactions set status=?,updated_at=? where id=?
INFO  SAV2001 availableBalance=950000
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Entity Lifecycle Callbacks ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Observer/Template: JPA invokes callbacks at fixed   │
  │   lifecycle points — entity reacts without caller   │
  │ Can centralize via @EntityListeners (shared listener)│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: callback does one thing (stamp/compute)          │
  │ O: add new cross-cutting rule via a listener class  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │         Transaction           │
  │  @PrePersist  onCreate()      │ set ref + createdAt
  │  @PostPersist afterCreate()   │ log/event
  │  @PreUpdate   onUpdate()      │ set updatedAt
  └───────────────────────────────┘
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │           Account             │
  │  @Transient availableBalance  │
  │  @PostLoad computeDerived()   │ balance - hold
  │  @PreRemove onDelete()        │ audit log
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── State/Order Diagram ──
  NEW ─@PrePersist→ INSERT ─@PostPersist→ MANAGED
  MANAGED(changed) ─@PreUpdate→ UPDATE ─@PostUpdate→ MANAGED
  loaded ─@PostLoad→ derived fields ready
  MANAGED ─@PreRemove→ DELETE ─@PostRemove→ gone

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. save(t) → flush → @PrePersist → INSERT → @PostPersist
  2. setStatus() → flush → @PreUpdate → UPDATE
  3. find(acct) → load → @PostLoad
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
JPA lifecycle callbacks are automatic hooks that fire at well-defined points in an entity's persistence lifecycle, so I never have to remember to call them from service code. PrePersist runs right before the insert and is where I set creation timestamps and generate reference numbers. PostPersist runs after the insert, when the generated id exists, so it is ideal for logging or publishing a domain event. PreUpdate runs before an update and is where I stamp the last-modified time, but an important detail is that it only fires if Hibernate's dirty checking actually detected a change. PostUpdate, PreRemove, and PostRemove wrap updates and deletes similarly.

PostLoad is the one developers forget. It runs immediately after an entity is populated from the database, which makes it the correct place to compute derived or transient fields. In our system an account carries a transient available-balance field that equals the current balance minus any held amount, and I compute it in PostLoad so every time the account is loaded the value is fresh without ever being stored.

In the National Bank of India transaction service, PrePersist guarantees every transaction gets a creation timestamp and a unique TXN reference before it is inserted, which removed a whole class of bugs where developers forgot to set those fields. PreUpdate records the modification time whenever a transaction's status changes, PreRemove writes an audit log before any account is deleted, and PostLoad presents the customer's available balance. This keeps cross-cutting persistence logic out of the service layer and in one predictable place.

The senior caution I always add is that callbacks must stay lightweight and must not call the EntityManager to run new queries or force a flush, because that can cause recursion or undefined behaviour inside the flush cycle. When the logic is cross-cutting across many entities, I move it into a dedicated listener class registered with EntityListeners so the rule lives in one place, and if a callback needs to trigger heavy work like sending notifications, I publish an event in PostPersist or PostUpdate and let an asynchronous consumer handle it rather than doing it inline.
